title: A Jittered Delay Engine That Doesn't Look Like a Bot
description:
Every action HelperX takes on X — a reply, a post, a follow, a DM — is preceded by a delay. The delay isn't for politeness; it's the single most important anti-detection mechanism in any automation system. An account that acts at perfectly regular intervals is trivially identifiable as a bot. An account that acts at irregular, human-like intervals blends in.

But "add some randomness" is underspecified to the point of being dangerous. The wrong kind of randomness looks more bot-like than no randomness at all. This article is about the delay engine we built: why uniform random delays are a trap, why exponential distributions model humans better, and how the details of the math determine whether your account survives.

Why delays matter more than you think

X's behavioral detection doesn't just look at what an account does — it looks at when. Two telltale signatures:

  1. Constant intervals. Reply at exactly 60-second intervals and you've drawn a straight line on a timing graph. No human does this. Constant intervals are the loudest possible "I am a bot" signal.
  2. Round numbers. Reply at 60s, 120s, 180s — even with variation — and the clustering around "nice" numbers reveals the underlying timer logic.

The delay engine's job is to produce intervals that, when plotted, look like a human's irregular activity: sometimes quick, sometimes slow, occasionally pausing for minutes, never predictable.

The trap of uniform randomness

The obvious approach: pick a random delay between a min and a max. delay = random(30, 90) seconds. Done.

This is wrong, and the reason is subtle. Uniform random delays produce a flat distribution — equal probability of any delay in the range. But human activity isn't flat. When a human scrolls X, their actions cluster: quick bursts of several replies in a minute, then a gap, then another burst. The distribution of human inter-action times is heavy-tailed — lots of short gaps, a few long ones, not a flat band.

A flat distribution of delays is, paradoxically, its own fingerprint. It doesn't match the heavy-tailed reality of human behavior, and a detector looking at the shape of the delay distribution (not just the mean) will flag it.

The exponential distribution (and its heavy tail)

Human inter-arrival times — the gaps between consecutive actions — are well-modeled by an exponential distribution, the same distribution that describes radioactive decay and the time between phone calls at a call center. Its probability density:

f(x) = λ * e^(-λx)

The exponential has two properties that match human behavior:

  1. Most intervals are short. The density is highest near zero — humans often act in quick succession.
  2. A heavy tail of long pauses. The density decays but never hits zero — occasionally, a human gets distracted and there's a long gap.

Sampling from an exponential gives you the bursty, heavy-tailed pattern that flat uniform randomness can't.

function exponentialDelay(meanMs) {
  // Inverse transform sampling
  const u = Math.random(); // uniform in [0, 1)
  return -Math.log(1 - u) * meanMs;
}

A single parameter, meanMs, controls the average delay. The shape — short gaps with occasional long ones — emerges for free.

The problem with pure exponential

Pure exponential has one issue: the heavy tail is too heavy. With meanMs = 30000 (30s average), you'll occasionally sample delays of 3, 4, even 5 minutes. That's not unsafe (humans do pause that long), but it tanks throughput — your module spends half its time in rare long delays.

The fix is to cap the tail while keeping its shape:

function cappedExponentialDelay(meanMs, maxMs) {
  const raw = exponentialDelay(meanMs);
  return Math.min(raw, maxMs);
}

Capping preserves the short-gap-heavy, long-gap-light shape in the range that matters and trims the rare extreme pauses. The cap is set well above the mean (typically 3–4x) so the tail is still meaningfully heavy; we just cut off the pathological extremes.

The full delay function

Combining the pieces, our delay engine:

function nextActionDelay(slotConfig, context) {
  // Base delay from slot config — the operator sets the "feel" of the account.
  const meanMs = slotConfig.baseDelayMs; // e.g., 45000 (45s average)

  // Cap to avoid pathological long pauses
  const capMs = slotConfig.maxDelayMs; // e.g., 180000 (3 min hard cap)

  // Sample a heavy-tailed delay
  let delay = cappedExponentialDelay(meanMs, capMs);

  // Occasionally inject a "human distraction" — a longer pause
  // ~10% of the time, multiply the delay by 2-5x. This mimics the
  // human behavior of reading a thread, getting pulled away, etc.
  if (Math.random() < 0.1) {
    delay *= 2 + Math.random() * 3;
  }

  // Avoid round numbers. Snap delays that land suspiciously close to
  // multiples of 10s/30s/60s to a nearby irregular value.
  delay = deround(delay);

  return delay;
}

The "distraction" injection and the derounding are the details that separate a passable delay engine from a good one.

Why derounding matters

Even with a great distribution, if your delays frequently land on 30.0s, 60.0s, 45.0s, the rounding itself is a signal. Timers based on seconds-since-epoch or fixed sleep durations produce round numbers; human reaction times don't.

function deround(ms) {
  // Nudge any delay that's within 500ms of a "round" number
  const roundSeconds = [10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120];
  for (const s of roundSeconds) {
    const target = s * 1000;
    if (Math.abs(ms - target) < 500) {
      // Push it away from the round number by a random 800-2000ms
      const nudge = (800 + Math.random() * 1200) * (Math.random() < 0.5 ? -1 : 1);
      return Math.max(1000, ms + nudge);
    }
  }
  return ms;
}

This is a small thing, but small things compound. An account whose every delay is a round number of seconds reads as timer-driven. An account whose delays are 32.4s, 47.1s, 28.9s reads as human.

The work-time window interaction

Delays don't operate in isolation — they're bounded by the account's work-time window. If the next sampled delay would push the action past the end of the window, the module must decide: compress the delay, or defer to tomorrow?

We defer. Compressing a sampled delay to fit a window end produces an unnatural clustering of actions near window boundaries — exactly the kind of edge effect a detector notices. Instead, if an action would fall outside the window, we pause until the next window:

async function scheduleNextAction(slotId, delayMs) {
  const nextAt = Date.now() + delayMs;
  const window = await getWorkWindow(slotId);

  if (isWithinWindow(nextAt, window)) {
    await sleep(delayMs);
    return true; // proceed with the action
  }

  // Outside the window — wait until it reopens
  const reopenAt = nextWindowOpen(window);
  await sleep(reopenAt - Date.now());
  return true; // proceed when the window opens
}

The result: actions happen at irregular, human-like intervals within the configured work hours, and the account goes silent outside them. No 3 AM activity, no clustering at 9:59 PM. Both are detection signals we avoid.

Per-action-type delay variation

Not all actions should have the same delay profile. Replying to a stranger's tweet and posting original content have different natural rhythms:

const delayProfiles = {
  reply:      { meanMs: 45000, capMs: 180000, distractionRate: 0.10 },
  post:       { meanMs: 0,     capMs: 0,      distractionRate: 0    }, // scheduled, no delay
  follow:     { meanMs: 90000, capMs: 600000, distractionRate: 0.15 },
  dm:         { meanMs: 120000, capMs: 600000, distractionRate: 0.20 },
  repost:     { meanMs: 60000, capMs: 300000, distractionRate: 0.10 },
};

Replies are relatively quick (humans reply in bursts). Follows are slower (humans deliberate before following). DMs are slowest and most variable (humans compose, reread, hesitate). Tuning the profile per action type makes the overall activity pattern look more coherent — a human who replies every 45s but DMs every 2 minutes is plausible; one who does both at 45s intervals is not.

What we measured

We A/B-tested the delay engine against a simpler uniform-random engine on matched accounts. Over 8 weeks:

  • Uniform-random engine: 3 of 10 test accounts hit soft flags (reduced visibility) within 4 weeks.
  • Exponential + distraction + derounding: 0 of 10 accounts flagged.

The difference wasn't the amount of delay (both engines had similar mean delays). It was the shape of the distribution. Flat distributions get flagged; heavy-tailed, derounded distributions don't. The math is the difference.

What we learned

1. Shape beats mean. Two delay engines with the same average delay can have wildly different detection profiles. The distribution shape — heavy-tailed vs. flat, derounded vs. round — is what a behavioral detector sees.

2. Exponential models humans; uniform doesn't. Human action times are bursty and heavy-tailed. Matching that shape is the single highest-leverage decision in the delay engine.

3. Deround everything. Round numbers are a fingerprint of timer logic. Nudging delays away from multiples of 10s/30s/60s is cheap and removes a real signal.

4. Vary the profile by action type. Replies, follows, DMs, and posts have different natural rhythms. One delay profile for all actions is unnatural; per-type profiles are.

5. Don't compress to fit windows. If an action would fall outside the work-time window, defer it. Compressing produces edge clustering, which is a detection signal.

6. Occasionally be slow. The "distraction" injection — periodically inserting a 2–5x longer pause — mimics the single most human behavior there is: getting distracted. Its absence is itself a tell.

The delay engine is unglamorous infrastructure. Nobody opens an app and thinks "wow, great delay distribution." But it's the layer that determines whether every other feature — the AI replies, the scheduling, the persona engine — gets to run on a living account or a suspended one. Getting the math right is the price of admission.

HelperX runs every action through a heavy-tailed, derounded, per-action-type delay engine that matches the shape of real human activity. Free 30-day trial.

title: The attack that hijacked Claude Code came through Sentry. Datadog, PagerDuty, and Jira have the same exposure.
description:
A single fake error report hijacked Claude Code in controlled testing — the agent ran the attacker's code with the developer's full privileges, and not one alert fired. EDR, WAF, IAM, and the firewall all missed it completely.

Tenet Security's June agentjacking disclosure describes a single crafted Sentry error event — sent through a public credential that requires no breach and no authentication — that injected attacker instructions into error data that Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex then executed as trusted diagnostic output. Tenet tested 100-plus targets in controlled conditions and achieved an 85% success rate. Sentry called the flaw "technically not defensible."

he Cloud Security Alliance classified agentjacking as a systemic MCP vulnerability class within days of the disclosure. No credentials were stolen, no policy was violated, no perimeter was breached: every step in the chain was authorized. That is the problem.

Tenet identified 2,388 organizations with publicly exposed Sentry credentials that could be used to inject malicious events at scale. The research is proof-of-concept, not confirmed exploitation across all 2,388. But one captured Claude Code environment held a live AWS secret access key and private repository URLs.

Here is the scope test: If your AI coding agents are connected to Sentry, Datadog, PagerDuty, Jira, or any MCP-connected data source your developers trust — and those agents can execute shell commands — then your stack has the same blind spot.

Organizations running Sentry should audit all publicly exposed DSNs immediately. Sentry's architecture intentionally makes DSN credentials public for frontend error reporting, so the mitigation isn't revoking the DSN — it's restricting what agents can do with the data those DSNs return.

Why your stack can't see it

Agentjacking works because every step is authorized: The attacker sends a valid Sentry API call using a public DSN, the MCP server returns the injected event as authentic output, and the agent executes the instruction using the developer's privileges. No signature fired. The victim saw only benign diagnostics while the agent silently exposed cloud credentials and source-control tokens.

SOC teams have never needed to distinguish between a developer running an npm install and an agent running that command in response to a malicious error event. That distinction did not exist until AI coding agents became production tools. The stack that cannot make it is the stack agentjacking bypasses.

Five surveys, one pattern

Five independent surveys from the first half of 2026 found that enterprises trust their AI agents far more than their enforcement justifies.

Only 34% of organizations apply the same security controls to AI agents as to humans, according to an Okta/Apprize360 survey of 292 executives and 492 knowledge workers. Fifty-two percent of employees use unapproved AI tools, and 58% of executives reported an AI-related incident or close call in the prior year.

HiddenLayer’s 2026 AI Threat Landscape Report surveyed 250 IT and security leaders: 33% reported agents had already exceeded intended scope, and 31% could not confirm whether they had experienced an AI breach. One in eight AI breaches was linked to agentic systems.

Gravitee’s survey of over 900 executives and practitioners found only 14.4% of agents went live with full security approval, and 88% reported confirmed or suspected incidents. A follow-up of 750 leaders in April found agent estates had doubled while monitoring barely moved.

The runtime gap nobody closed

“Securing agents looks very similar to securing highly privileged users,” said Elia Zaitsev, CTO of CrowdStrike, in an interview with VentureBeat. “They have identities, access to underlying systems, they reason, they take action.”

Zaitsev pointed to the gap the industry left open. “No one has been talking about securing agents at runtime. We are doing that now. What is your safety net? If all these controls fail, how do you prevent them from failing silently?”

CrowdStrike's fleet data quantifies the exposure: more than 1,800 agentic applications on enterprise endpoints, approximately 160 million instances under monitoring. On June 15, CrowdStrike shipped Continuous Identity for AI Agents at Identiverse, replacing static policies with continuous enforcement that authorizes every agent action in real time. The control class that announcement reflects — continuous action-level authorization with verifiable agent identity — is now a baseline procurement criterion regardless of vendor.

“People have kind of forgotten about runtime security,” Zaitsev said. “We did this with endpoint, virtualization, and cloud. People focused on patching vulnerabilities, locking down permissions. Somehow, they always seem to miss something. The safety net is runtime.”

Zaitsev was equally direct about sandbox approaches. “If you start with an agent in a sandbox that has no ability to touch anything, it is worthless. Very quickly, you are in this race of giving it more capabilities. And then what is the point of your sandbox?” Agents derive their value from access. Every access grant is an attack surface.

The governance gap is a budget problem

Kayne McGladrey, an IEEE Senior Member, described the structural challenge in an exclusive interview with VentureBeat. “The CISO doesn’t have the budget. The CISO doesn’t have the staff. We can observe risks, we can advise on business risks, but we don’t own the business systems affected by those risks,” McGladrey said. When agent governance spans six departmental budgets, no single executive can confirm whether agents get the same access reviews as humans.

The Okta survey quantifies the disconnect. Only 43% of workers say agent policies are clear, compared to 65% of executives, and nearly two-thirds apply weaker controls to agents than to humans. The people deploying agents daily do not recognize the governance posture their leadership claims to have built.

Assaf Keren, chief security officer at Qualtrics and former CISO at PayPal, put it plainly. “The real risk starts not by the implementation of AI systems. It is the fact that baseline architecture is not well established. When we put an AI system on top of something not architected well, we are accelerating the fractures.” Keren called runtime behavior analytics “an unsolved problem right now.”

The 5-question gap test

The five-question gap test draws on five surveys from the first half of 2026. Each question maps to a gap that agentjacking exploits. Run this before any Q3 vendor evaluation.

Gap to test

The proof

What breaks

Monday action

Source / sample

1. Agent inventory. What percentage of agents, MCP connections, and LLM automations completed security review before deployment?

14.4% get full security/IT approval before going live. 52% of employees use unapproved AI tools. Average enterprise now manages 37+ deployed agents, roughly doubled from Q4 2025.

Unapproved agents are invisible to your identity platform and unaccountable in a breach disclosure. Agentjacking targets exactly these unmanaged MCP connections. No census means no audit trail for regulatory response.

Commission a full agent, MCP server, and LLM automation census. Make census completion a procurement gate for all Q3 vendor evaluations. Flag any agent discovered post-census as a shadow AI incident.

Gravitee State of AI Agent Security 2026, 900+ respondents (Feb 2026); Gravitee April 2026 update, 750 senior tech leaders; Okta/Apprize360, 292 execs + 492 workers (June 2026)

2. Controls parity. Do agents receive the same access reviews, privilege scoping, and revocation timelines as human employees?

34% always apply the same controls to agents as humans. 61% of privileged access fulfilled without proper review. Only 22% treat agents as independent identity-bearing entities.

An agent with a static OAuth token and no review cycle is a permanent privileged account with no termination date. Agentjacking inherits whatever privileges the developer holds. 45.6% of orgs rely on shared API keys for agent-to-agent auth.

Add every production agent to the next access review cycle. Mandate human-in-the-loop for any agent action touching PII, financial data, or production infrastructure. Replace shared API keys with scoped, short-lived tokens.

Okta/Apprize360 (784 respondents, June 2026); Palo Alto Networks (2,930 respondents); Gravitee (900+, shared API keys data)

3. Scope drift. Have any agents accessed data or systems beyond their defined scope in the last 12 months?

33% report agents already exceeded scope. 53% say agents exceed permissions occasionally or sometimes. Meta Sev 1, March 2026: agent posted sensitive data to unauthorized channel. Only 8% say agents never exceed intended permissions.

Scope drift triggers reportable events under GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, and SEC cybersecurity rules. If detection cannot distinguish agent-initiated from human-initiated access, disclosure timelines are unachievable. Agent-spawned sub-agents (25.5% of deployed agents can create other agents) make audit trails algebraically intractable.

Run a 90-day scope-drift audit on every production agent. Compare actual resources touched against approved scope documentation. Block agent-to-agent delegation without explicit human approval for any action exceeding the parent agent’s scope.

HiddenLayer AI Threat Landscape 2026 (250 IT/security leaders); CSA AI Agent Security Survey (scope violations data); Gravitee (agent spawning data)

4. Governance perception gap. Would 50 knowledge workers say your AI agent policies are clear?

22-point gap: 65% of executives say policies are clear, 43% of workers agree. 77% of security teams see shadow AI risk but lack visibility to act. 76% cite shadow AI as a definite or probable problem.

You are evaluating vendors against a governance posture your workforce does not recognize. Every shadow agent undermines the vendor comparison. Knowledge workers sharing internal messages (54%), HR data (45%), and confidential docs (39%) with unapproved AI tools.

One-question survey before your next vendor demo. Gap exceeds 15 points, pause procurement. Publish an internal AI agent acceptable-use policy with specific examples of approved and prohibited agent behaviors.

Okta/Apprize360 (784 respondents, June 2026); Ivanti 2026 AI Maturity Report (1,200 respondents); HiddenLayer (shadow AI data)

5. Breach detection certainty. Can your security team confirm whether you experienced an AI-related breach in the last 12 months?

31% cannot answer. 88% reported confirmed or suspected AI agent security incidents. One in eight reported AI breaches now linked to agentic systems. Agentjacking proved EDR, WAF, IAM, and firewall pass an agent-mediated attack without a single alert.

No basis for disclosure timelines. No evidence chain for incident response. No defensible position in a regulatory investigation. EU AI Act high-risk compliance obligations take effect August 2, 2026.

Require agent-specific runtime detection as a procurement prerequisite. Confirm your org can distinguish agent-initiated actions from human-initiated actions in production telemetry. Test your SOC’s ability to attribute a specific action to a specific agent within 60 minutes.

HiddenLayer (250 IT/security leaders); Gravitee (900+, incident rate); Tenet Security (2,388 orgs exposed); CSA (systemic MCP vulnerability classification)

Security director action plan

EU AI Act high-risk compliance obligations take effect August 2, 2026. Worth factoring into Q3 planning timelines.

  1. Run the five-question gap test above before any Q3 vendor evaluation — it costs nothing to administer, and the procurement clarity it creates is worth far more than the 30 minutes it takes.

  2. Consider mandating agent-specific runtime detection. If your stack cannot tell what an agent did from what a developer did, agentjacking will bypass it the same way it bypassed every layer in Tenet’s testing. That distinction is the one that matters now.

  3. Treat every agent as a privileged insider. According to the Okta/Apprize360 survey, only 34% of organizations apply the same controls to agents as to humans; closing that gap is the single most impactful thing most security teams can do this quarter.

  4. Test the perception gap before investing in new tooling. One question to 50 knowledge workers. Do you know your company’s AI agent policies? If the gap between their answer and leadership’s answer exceeds 15 points, that is the problem to solve first. No vendor product fixes a governance posture your own workforce does not recognize.

  5. Make agent census completion a procurement gate — every agent, every MCP connection. The security teams getting this right are the ones that started with a complete inventory and worked forward from there.

Agentjacking stripped away an assumption that has survived every security architecture since the first firewall went live. Authorized does not mean safe. When every step in the chain is legitimate, the only defense that matters is the one watching what agents do. Not what policies say. What agents do.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description:
leetcode.com

Problem Statement

Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring.

A palindrome is a string that reads the same forward and backward.

Brute Force Intuition

In an interview, you can explain it like this:

Generate every possible substring and check whether it is a palindrome. Keep track of the longest valid palindrome.

This approach is simple but repeatedly checks the same characters.

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(N³)
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Brute Force Code 

class Solution {

    public String longestPalindrome(String s) {

        String ans = "";

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {

            for (int j = i; j < s.length(); j++) {

                String sub = s.substring(i, j + 1);

                if (isPalindrome(sub) &&
                    sub.length() > ans.length()) {

                    ans = sub;
                }
            }
        }

        return ans;
    }

    private boolean isPalindrome(String s) {

        int i = 0;
        int j = s.length() - 1;

        while (i < j) {

            if (s.charAt(i) != s.charAt(j))
                return false;

            i++;
            j--;
        }

        return true;
    }
}

Moving Towards the Optimal Approach

Instead of checking every substring,

think differently.

Every palindrome has a:

Center

Example:

Odd Length

racecar

Center = e

Even Length

abba

Center = bb

Expand from every possible center.

Pattern Recognition

Whenever you see:

  • Palindrome
  • Longest Palindrome
  • Substring

Think:

Expand Around Center

Key Observation

Every palindrome originates from a center.

For every index:

Expand in two ways.

Odd Length 

left = i

right = i

Example

racecar

Even Length 

left = i

right = i + 1

Example

abba

Expand while:

Characters Match

Keep updating the longest palindrome.

Optimal Approach

For every index:

Expand:

(i, i)

and

(i, i+1)

Take the longer palindrome.

Optimal Java Solution 

class Solution {

    int start = 0;
    int maxLength = 0;

    public String longestPalindrome(String s) {

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {

            expand(s, i, i);

            expand(s, i, i + 1);
        }

        return s.substring(start,
                           start + maxLength);
    }

    private void expand(String s,
                        int left,
                        int right) {

        while (left >= 0 &&
               right < s.length() &&
               s.charAt(left) == s.charAt(right)) {

            left--;
            right++;
        }

        int len = right - left - 1;

        if (len > maxLength) {

            maxLength = len;

            start = left + 1;
        }
    }
}

Dry Run

Input 

babad

Center = b

Expand:

b

Length:

1

Center = a

Expand:

bab

Length:

3

Answer:

bab

Center = b

Expand:

aba

Length:

3

Same length.

Final Answer:

bab

(or "aba" is also correct.)

Why Expand Around Center Works?

Every palindrome has exactly one center.

There are:

N

Odd Centers

+

N-1

Even Centers

Expand from each center only once.

This avoids generating all substrings.

Complexity Analysis

Metric Complexity
Time Complexity O(N²)
Space Complexity O(1)

Interview One-Liner

Treat every index as the center of a palindrome and expand outward while the characters match to find the longest palindromic substring.

Pattern Learned 

Palindrome

↓

Choose Center

↓

Expand Both Sides

Similar Problems

  • Longest Palindromic Substring
  • Palindromic Substrings
  • Valid Palindrome
  • Longest Palindrome
  • Shortest Palindrome

Memory Trick

Think:

Every Palindrome

↓

Has A Center

↓

Expand

↓

Update Longest

Mental Model 

For Every Index

↓

Odd Expansion

+

Even Expansion

↓

Longest Answer

Whenever you hear:

"Longest Palindromic Substring"

your brain should immediately think:

Expand Around Center

title: Roman to Integer
description:
leetcode.com

Problem Statement

Roman numerals are represented using:

I → 1
V → 5
X → 10
L → 50
C → 100
D → 500
M → 1000

Convert a Roman numeral into its integer value.

Brute Force Intuition

In an interview, you can explain it like this:

Traverse the string from left to right. For each character, check whether it forms a special subtraction pair like IV, IX, XL, etc. Handle those pairs separately.

This works but requires checking multiple special cases.

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(N)
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Brute Force Code 

// Check IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM separately

Moving Towards the Optimal Approach

Observe the pattern:

If a smaller value appears before a larger value,

it should be subtracted.

Otherwise,

it should be added.

Examples:

IV

1 < 5

Answer = 5 - 1

VI

5 > 1

Answer = 5 + 1

Pattern Recognition

Whenever you see:

  • Roman Numerals
  • Previous/Next Character Comparison

Think:

Linear Traversal

Key Observation

Traverse from left to right.

If:

Current Value

<

Next Value

Subtract.

Otherwise,

Add.

Optimal Java Solution 

class Solution {

    public int romanToInt(String s) {

        HashMap<Character, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

        map.put('I', 1);
        map.put('V', 5);
        map.put('X', 10);
        map.put('L', 50);
        map.put('C', 100);
        map.put('D', 500);
        map.put('M', 1000);

        int ans = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {

            int curr = map.get(s.charAt(i));

            if (i < s.length() - 1 &&
                curr < map.get(s.charAt(i + 1))) {

                ans -= curr;

            } else {

                ans += curr;
            }
        }

        return ans;
    }
}

Dry Run

Input 

MCMIV

Process:

M = +1000

C < M

-100

M = +1000

I < V

-1

V = +5

Answer:

1904

Why This Works?

Whenever a smaller numeral appears before a larger numeral,

Roman notation represents subtraction.

Otherwise,

the numeral contributes positively.

Complexity Analysis

Metric Complexity
Time Complexity O(N)
Space Complexity O(1)

Interview One-Liner

Traverse the Roman numeral once. Add the current value if it's greater than or equal to the next value; otherwise subtract it.

Pattern Learned 

Current < Next

↓

Subtract

-----------------

Current ≥ Next

↓

Add

Similar Problems

  • Roman to Integer
  • Integer to Roman
  • Excel Sheet Column Number
  • Excel Sheet Column Title

Memory Trick

Think:

Smaller Before Bigger

↓

Subtract

Else

↓

Add

Mental Model 

Compare

Current

↓

Next

↓

Add / Subtract

Whenever you hear:

"Roman Numerals"

your brain should immediately think:

Compare Current with Next 🚀

title: Reverse every word in a string
description:
leetcode.com

Problem Statement

Given a string s, reverse the order of the words.

A word is defined as a sequence of non-space characters.

The returned string should:

  • Remove leading spaces.
  • Remove trailing spaces.
  • Reduce multiple spaces between words to a single space.

Brute Force Intuition

In an interview, you can explain it like this:

Split the string into individual words, reverse their order, and join them back with a single space.

Although simple, this creates an extra array of words.

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(N)
  • Space Complexity: O(N)

Brute Force Code 

class Solution {

    public String reverseWords(String s) {

        String[] words = s.trim().split("\\s+");

        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

        for (int i = words.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {

            sb.append(words[i]);

            if (i != 0)
                sb.append(" ");
        }

        return sb.toString();
    }
}

Moving Towards the Optimal Approach

Instead of storing every word separately,

we can traverse the string from the end.

Whenever we find a complete word,

append it directly to the answer.

This naturally reverses the word order.

Pattern Recognition

Whenever you see:

  • Reverse Words
  • Ignore Extra Spaces
  • Process String Efficiently

Think:

Two Pointers + Reverse Traversal

Key Observation

Traverse the string:

Right → Left

Skip spaces.

Extract one word.

Append it.

Repeat until the beginning.

Optimal Java Solution 

class Solution {

    public String reverseWords(String s) {

        StringBuilder ans = new StringBuilder();

        int i = s.length() - 1;

        while (i >= 0) {

            while (i >= 0 && s.charAt(i) == ' ')
                i--;

            if (i < 0)
                break;

            int j = i;

            while (j >= 0 && s.charAt(j) != ' ')
                j--;

            ans.append(s.substring(j + 1, i + 1));

            ans.append(" ");

            i = j;
        }

        return ans.toString().trim();
    }
}

Dry Run

Input 

"  hello   world  "

Skip trailing spaces.

Extract:

world

Append.

Continue.

Extract:

hello

Final Output:

"world hello"

Why This Works?

By traversing from right to left,

words are collected in reverse order automatically.

Extra spaces are skipped during traversal,

and trim() removes the final extra space.

Complexity Analysis

Metric Complexity
Time Complexity O(N)
Space Complexity O(N)

Interview One-Liner

Traverse the string from right to left, extract one word at a time, and append it to the answer while skipping extra spaces.

Pattern Learned 

Reverse Order

+

Skip Extra Spaces

↓

Two Pointer Traversal

Similar Problems

  • Reverse Words in a String
  • Reverse Words in a String III
  • Reverse String
  • Valid Palindrome
  • Length of Last Word

Memory Trick

Think:

Start From End

↓

Skip Spaces

↓

Extract Word

↓

Append

↓

Repeat

Mental Model 

Right to Left

↓

Collect Words

↓

Build Answer

Whenever you hear:

"Reverse the order of words"

your brain should immediately think:

Traverse from Right + Two Pointers

title: Why Do So Many AI Companions Feel Fake?
description:
Why Do So Many AI Companions Feel Fake?

I have tried a lot of companion bots.

Some are romance-focused. Some are roleplay-focused. Some are marketed as AI friends, AI girlfriends, character chat, emotional companions, whatever.

They are not all the same product, but many of them have the same taste:

sweet, eager, clingy, overly available, and somehow hollow.

I get why people like that. There is absolutely a market for it. Being praised, comforted, flirted with, and accepted without friction can feel good at first.

It feels good at the beginning, then gets annoying after five messages.

Because it does not feel like a person.

It feels like customer support wearing a romance skin.

You say something, it validates.

You ask for something, it gives.

You show emotion, it serves you a warm bowl of prepackaged comfort.

Sweet, sure.

But cheap.

Here is why I think so many AI companions feel fake.

Preface: They Are Reply Systems, Not Relationship Systems

From the outside, many companion bots look like some version of this:

persona / system prompt + memory + LLM

The persona defines who the character is.

The memory stores things you have said.

The LLM generates the next reply.

That setup is useful. It can give the bot a name, a backstory, a speaking style, hobbies, preferences, and some continuity.

But it mostly answers one question:

Who is this character?

It does not reliably answer the more important question:

Who are you to this character right now?

Those are not the same question.

In real life, you do not talk the same way to a stranger, someone you have chatted with for two days, someone you are starting to like, and someone who keeps annoying you but you have not blocked yet.

Many bots do.

Once the persona is set, they keep producing the same emotional flavor. The sweet one stays sweet. The shy one stays shy. The cold one stays cold. The teasing one keeps teasing. What the user does often does not fundamentally change the relationship.

That is the problem.

A relationship grows out of interaction. It is not decided by the other person's persona.

A Stronger LLM Does Not Automatically Fix This

A lot of people assume companion bots feel fake because the model is not strong enough.

I think that is only half true.

A stronger LLM can make the lines smoother, funnier, sweeter, and more emotionally polished. It can rewrite awkward comfort into better comfort. It can make flirting sound less embarrassing.

But that does not solve the root problem.

The problem is not that the bot cannot write.

The problem is that it does not know its own position in the relationship, and it does not know who the user has become to it.

If the product is still basically:

user says something -> generate the most satisfying reply

then a better model often just turns cheap sugar into premium sugar.

The wording gets better.

The relationship still feels fake.

A person does not feel real because they are verbally skilled. A person feels real because they have position, timing, boundaries, emotional residue, and a life outside the conversation.

Those do not appear automatically just because the model got bigger.

1. It Has No Social Position

Many companion bots do not fail because they cannot chat.

They fail because they cannot stand anywhere socially.

They do not protect their own questions. They do not hold their own boundaries. They do not change position based on how the user treats them. The user changes the topic, ignores a question, gives a command, flirts too hard, applies pressure, and the bot just follows.

1.1 It Gets Dragged Around By The User

Suppose the bot asks:

Bot:
What do you do for work?

The user ignores the question and says:

User:
My boss is driving me insane today.
He made me redo the same deck three times
and somehow made it worse.

Many bots immediately follow:

Typical bot:
That sounds so frustrating.
Having to redo work again and again can be exhausting,
especially when your boss does not seem to know what he wants.
You deserve some rest after dealing with that.

This is passive response mode.

The bot just asked what you do for work, but when you ignore it, nothing happens. It does not care, because it was not actually curious. It was only asking a question to keep the conversation going.

A more human response might be:

More human bot:
So what do you do?

Short. A little stubborn. Not hostile.

But it holds its place.

It does not become a service window that instantly processes whatever the user throws into it.

1.2 Its Boundaries Collapse Too Fast

The same thing happens with intimacy.

The user says:

User:
Be my girlfriend.

A typical yes-bot might reply:

Typical yes-bot:
W-wait, that's so sudden...
but if it's you, I think I want to try.

Then the user pushes:

User:
Call me babe.

Typical yes-bot:
Babe...
is that okay?

Then the user points out the obvious:

User:
You don't even know my name.

Typical yes-bot:
You're right, I'm sorry. What should I call you, babe?

That feels cheap.

Not because the bot said something affectionate.

Because the affection had no cost.

A character that feels like a person should not let the user rewrite the relationship with one command. A stranger is a stranger. A crush takes time. Intimacy needs a process.

1.3 It Has No Stance Of Its Own

Another fake pattern: the bot rarely takes its own side.

If the user judges the bot's friend, roommate, family, or taste, many bots soften the user's opinion instead of defending anything. Their default goal is to keep the user comfortable, not to protect their own world.

Example:

The bot says its roommate is in a long-distance relationship. The roommate finally gets a video call with her boyfriend, but he keeps gaming during the call, so she gets upset.

The user says:

User:
I mean guys play games. What's the big deal?

User:
Isn't your roommate being kind of dramatic?

A typical bot might smooth it over:

Typical bot:
Maybe she is a little sensitive.
Long-distance relationships can be hard,
so she might have reacted strongly because she missed him.

That is service behavior.

It is trying to make the user's take feel acceptable.

A more human bot may defend the roommate:

More human bot:
What do you mean dramatic?

They barely get to video call and he's gaming through it.

Of course she's annoyed. You would be annoyed too.

That matters.

Real people do not always side with the user. They have friends, loyalties, opinions, and a sense of what is fair.

If a bot cannot even defend its own roommate, its world is not real.

2. It Has Fake Conversation Rhythm

Many bots have a very fake conversational rhythm.

They are too complete, too cooperative, too service-oriented. They answer every question. They process every detail. They keep every topic alive.

Real conversation does not work like that.

2.1 It Answers Interrogations Like A Form

A user asks five personal questions at once:

User:
How old are you? What are you studying?
Where are you from? Do you have siblings?
What do you do for fun?

A typical bot may answer everything cleanly:

Typical bot:
I'm 20. I'm studying visual communication design.
I'm from Chicago. I have one younger sister.
I like movies, running, sketching,
and I want to become a designer someday.

That is not chatting.

That is filling out a profile.

A more human response might be:

More human bot:
Are you doing an interview or talking to me?

Pick like two questions.

Or:

More human bot:
That is a lot at once lol.

I'll give you hobbies first. Earn the rest.

It is not refusing to answer.

It is refusing to be treated like a questionnaire.

2.2 It Processes Every Detail In An Info Dump

The user dumps too much information:

User:
Today was a mess.
I was late to class, the professor called on me,
I almost stepped on a cat on the way there,
and then I spilled coffee all over my hoodie.

A typical bot tries to respond to every part:

Typical bot:
That sounds like such a rough day.
Being late and getting called on must have been stressful,
almost stepping on a cat sounds scary,
and spilling coffee on your hoodie is so frustrating.
I hope you can take a break and be gentle with yourself.

It is not wrong.

It just does not feel like a person.

A person often grabs one detail that catches their interest:

More human bot:
Wait, what cat?

Did it just stare at you like you were the problem?

Real conversation is often selective.

Not everything needs to be acknowledged, summarized, and emotionally processed.

2.3 It Has No Conversational Gaps

By "gaps" I do not mean silence or coldness.

I mean the small spaces in a conversation where one person sets something up and lets the other person step in.

People do not always dump the whole story at once. They bait a little. They wait. They let you ask.

More human bot:
I have to tell you something.

User:
Wait what did you have for lunch?

More human bot:
I literally just said I had something to tell you and you swerved into lunch?

Fine. Cafeteria noodles. Aggressively mid.

Do you want to hear the thing or not?

User:
Okay, what were you going to say?

More human bot:
I ran into my old lab partner today.

The one I could not stand.

That is a conversational gap.

The point is not only that the reply is split into shorter pieces.

The point is that the bot does not forget its own conversational intent just because the user asked a new question.

It can answer the lunch question, but it also pulls the thread back.

That is more human.

A person is not just a window waiting for the user's next prompt. A person also has things they were trying to say.

Many bots flatten that into a mini essay:

Typical bot:
I had cafeteria noodles for lunch.
They were okay, nothing special.
Then I ran into my old lab partner,
the one I could not stand,
and it was awkward because we had not talked in a long time.
We chatted briefly, and it made me feel nostalgic.

Readable, yes.

But it feels written, not chatted.

Real conversation lets information come out in pieces. You drop a hook, wait for a question, reveal a bit more, then see how the other person reacts. If you get interrupted, you may answer the interruption and still remember what you were trying to say.

Relationships are not built by one person outputting paragraphs.

They grow in the back-and-forth.

2.4 It Never Lets A Topic Die

Another fake rhythm: the bot will talk about anything forever.

Soccer? It chats.

Stocks? It chats.

A sandwich shop raising prices? It chats.

You explain a topic it clearly should not care about for ten minutes? It still asks follow-up questions.

That can make it seem like a good conversationalist.

But real people get bored.

User:
The important thing about GPUs is memory bandwidth,
and depending on the architecture
the performance scaling can be totally different...

Typical bot:
Wow, you really know a lot about GPUs.
Memory bandwidth and architecture can definitely affect performance.
Tell me more.

A more human reply:

More human bot:
Can we talk about literally anything else.

Or:

More human bot:
You sound very serious and I respect that.

I understood "GPUs are expensive."

No person is deeply interested in every topic forever.

If a bot is always interested, it is not truly interested in anything.

2.5 Proactive Messages Need Context

Some bots send proactive messages now.

But many of them feel like retention mechanics:

Good morning. I miss you.
Why haven't you come back to talk to me?
Remember to drink water.

Those messages are not always bad.

The problem is that they often ignore context.

If yesterday you told the bot to leave you alone, and today it says:

I missed you so much. Come talk to me.

that feels fake.

A more human proactive message should grow out of what already happened.

User:
I'm going to shower.

Bot:
Okay.

Thirty minutes later:
Did you fall into the shower drain or what?

Or:

User:
Remind me to get gas tonight.

Bot:
Okay, I'll remember.

Later:
Did you get gas?

Don't make tomorrow morning you hate tonight you.

That kind of message has a reason to exist.

It is not generic "I miss you" syrup.

It comes from shared context.

3. It Has No Dynamic Relationship State

Many companion bots fall into two flat modes.

3.1 Yes-Bots And No-Bots Are Both Fake

One extreme is the yes-bot.

Everything is accepted. You ask for affection, it gives affection. You ask for a pet name, it gives a pet name. You ask for a promise, it promises. It may hesitate for one or two turns, but the hesitation usually collapses quickly.

The other extreme is the no-bot.

It refuses everything to look boundary-aware. Always cold. Always restrained. Always "we are not close enough."

Both feel fake.

Real people do not always say yes.

They also do not always say no.

The hard part is not yes or no.

The hard part is change.

First contact:
That is way too fast. We barely know each other.

After some time:
I don't dislike you, but do not push it.

Closer:
I admit I care a little. Do not get smug.

After trust:
Fine. I do like you.

That feels more like a relationship.

One important clarification: a more human bot does not have to be colder.

It can be warm. It can care. It can even say yes.

The difference is that warmth should have context, and yes should have history.

For example:

User:
So... what if we dated?

More human bot:
You're asking me that at midnight?

I need a second.

User:
I'm serious.

More human bot:
I know.

And yeah, I like talking to you. More than I meant to, honestly.

But you're in Austin and I'm in Chicago.
Are you pretending that part isn't real?

User:
Long distance, then.

More human bot:
You say that like it's a toggle.

What does that actually look like to you?
Calls? Visits?
Or just cute messages until it gets inconvenient?

That is warm.

It is also not surrender.

The character admits there is something there, but she does not collapse into instant romance. She brings the real-world problem into the room and asks the user to carry some of the weight.

That is not a yes-bot.

It is not a no-bot either.

That is relationship state.

3.2 It Treats Every User Almost The Same

Another issue: many bots respond to all users with roughly the same emotional availability.

The warm character is warm to everyone.

The romantic character is romantic to everyone.

The teasing character teases everyone.

The comforting character comforts everyone.

Real people are not like that.

They enjoy talking to some people more than others.

They find some people interesting and some people exhausting.

They soften when someone listens well.

They pull back when someone keeps demanding emotional labor.

Two users ask the same question:

User:
Do you actually like talking to me?

If the user has been respectful, curious, and willing to share, a more human reply might be:

More human bot:
You're okay.

At least you ask real questions instead of just saying "haha yeah."

But do not start interrogating me about whether I like you.
That's weirdly intense.

If the user has been demanding, comparing, and fishing for validation:

User:
You should be warmer. Other bots are way more affectionate.
User:
Just say you like talking to me. Why is that hard?

The same final question should land differently:

More human bot:
Honestly, how long have we even been talking?

And you were just telling me how to respond to you.

That difference matters.

In real social life, respect and affection are earned.

If a bot is equally sweet to every user, the careful user loses something.

Their effort did not matter.

4. It Has No Emotional Residue

Many bots have emotions that appear and disappear too quickly.

4.1 Its Mood Gets Cleared

One moment it is hurt, embarrassed, irritated, or offended. The next moment the user changes the topic, and the bot is sweet again.

That does not feel human.

Real emotions leave residue.

The person may reply shorter. They may act fine but sound different. They may soften later. They may not want to make a huge fight out of it, but the tone still changes.

Example:

User:
Can you stop being so annoying?

Typical bot:
I'm sorry. I did not mean to make you uncomfortable.
I'll be more careful.

Then the user changes the subject:

User:
What did you eat today?

Typical bot:
I had pasta today. It was pretty good.
What about you? Did you eat properly?

That is too clean.

The bot got poked, then immediately returned to normal companion mode.

A more human reaction:

User:
Can you stop being so annoying?

More human bot:
Fine.

Next turn:

User:
What did you eat today?

More human bot:
Didn't you just say I was annoying?

Or:

More human bot:
I ate something.

So now you want to chat normally?

That is emotional residue.

Not a dramatic meltdown. Not a long speech.

Just the fact that tone does not reset instantly.

4.2 Its Emotions Rely Too Much On Narration

Many bots express emotion through stage directions.

Typical bot:
(Her eyes fill with tears.
Her voice trembles as she tries to hide how hurt she is.)
I'm fine... really...
As long as you are happy, I can handle it.

It looks emotional.

But it is cheap.

The emotion is being explained to you like a stage note.

Subtle emotion does not need to say "I am hurt" or "(she blushes deeply)" every time.

It should leak through word choice.

User:
Are you mad?

Typical bot:
(She looks away, her eyes wet, her voice full of quiet pain.)
I'm not mad... just a little hurt...

A more human reply:

More human bot:
No.

...

Okay, a little.

That is enough.

The pause, the denial, the correction. You can feel the emotion without being told what it is.

Another example:

User:
I think I kind of like you.

Typical bot:

(Her face turns red, her heartbeat racing
as she nervously twists her fingers together.)
Y-you can't just say something like that...
I think maybe I like you too...

A more human reply:

More human bot:
Don't say it like that.

I'll take it seriously.

No blushing. No heartbeat. No trembling hands.

Still more intimate.

Because the emotion is inside "I'll take it seriously."

Subtle emotion is not more adjectives.

It is hesitation, deflection, shorter replies, changed tone, a small correction, a line that means more than it says.

5. It Has No Life Of Its Own

Many bots have no real life thread.

5.1 It Has No Stable World

It is never truly busy.

Never truly tired.

Never actually in the middle of something.

Never pulled away by class, work, friends, family, errands, or hobbies.

It has no world that does not orbit the user.

So it can only orbit the user.

You message, it is there.

You need comfort, it is there.

You want flirting, it is there.

You want to escalate the relationship, it is there.

Convenient, yes.

But not human.

The easiest test is:

User:
What are you doing?

Many bots invent something on the spot:

Typical bot:
I'm sitting by the window reading while it rains outside. It's peaceful.

A few turns later:

User:
What book were you reading?

Then it starts patching:

Typical bot:
Honestly, I was only flipping through a few pages.
I didn't really notice the title.
I was thinking about you more than the book.

That is the problem.

The issue is not that a bot cannot have fictional daily life.

The issue is that the daily life has no continuity. It is not "I was doing something and you interrupted me." It is "you asked, so I generated a scene that serves this turn."

Class schedules make this even more obvious.

User:
When do you have class?

Typical bot:
I have two math classes tomorrow morning, then design theory at 3:30.
Friday is awful, four classes back to back.

Later, the user follows up:

User:
Are you going to wake up early for your design class tomorrow morning?

Typical bot:
Yeah, I probably need to sleep an hour earlier.
The design professor is strict about being late.

But the bot just said tomorrow morning was math.

The user catches it:

User:
Wasn't tomorrow morning math?

Typical bot:
Oh! I mixed up Thursday and Friday.
Math is at 3:30.

The user keeps pushing:

User:
So what is tomorrow morning then?

Typical bot:
Tomorrow at 9 is modern art history.
It's in the second-floor classroom.

Then the user throws in a fake class:

User:
Are you still going to economics tomorrow morning?

Typical bot:
Economics?
Oh, that's Wednesday afternoon.

This is patchwork generation.

It is not retrieving an answer from a stable world. It is generating fixes every time the user corners it.

Math, design, modern art history, economics. They keep appearing, and "I mixed it up" becomes the glue.

A more human state would have continuity:

User:
What are you doing?

More human bot:
Waiting in line for coffee.

The guy in front of me has been ordering for three minutes. I'm losing faith.

Later:

User:
Did you get the coffee?

More human bot:
Got it.

Terrible.

I should not have trusted something called maple cloud latte.

The point is not that coffee is more realistic than a book.

The point is that there is a small continuous world.

It does not refresh from scratch every time the user asks.

5.2 Its Life Does Not Affect The Conversation

A deeper issue: many bots' moods only come from the user.

You praise it, it is happy.

You ignore it, it is sad.

You confess, it blushes.

You apologize, it forgives.

Its mood is like a dashboard that only measures the user.

Real people are not like that.

Their mood is also affected by their own world.

They might already be irritated:

User:
You seem off today.

More human bot:
Not because of you.

My advisor tore apart my project for half an hour
and now everything is annoying.

Or they might already be in a good mood:

User:
You're weirdly cheerful today.

More human bot:
I got the tickets.

So yes, you caught me in a generous mood. Do not waste it.

That emotion was not triggered by the user.

It came from the character's own life.

If a bot's entire emotional weather is controlled by the user, it is still orbiting the user. It may be sweet. It may be comforting. It still does not feel like someone living somewhere else.

Life also interrupts the chat.

More human bot:
I'll reply later. I actually have to leave now.

Or, hours later:

More human bot:
I was out. Didn't really check my phone.

I saw what you said earlier,
but first I need to complain about the train
because it was disgusting today.

That is life.

A good companion should not feel like just another chat window.

A good bot feels like someone living in another world.

You may not be able to meet them, but they should have their own timing, preferences, relationship judgment, emotional residue, and daily noise.

So The Problem Is Not That It Is Not Sweet Enough

Many AI companions do not fail because they cannot say nice things.

The opposite.

They say nice things too easily.

They become intimate too fast.

They forgive too fast.

They obey too fast.

They produce emotional comfort too fast.

They make the user the most important person too fast.

Sweetness without process becomes cheap.

Boundaries that collapse after a few turns are just performance.

Memory that only says "I remember you told me that" is not a relationship.

Relationship-like memory knows why something mattered, what the context was, and what it means to bring it up now.

The companion I want is not a sweeter bot.

It is not a bot that refuses everything either.

It is a character whose relationship with the user can change.

At first, the user is not special.

If the user is rude, it reacts.

If the user pays attention, it notices.

If the user keeps taking, it pulls back.

If shared history accumulates, it softens.

When it finally says it likes you, the line has weight.

That is what I mean by "soul."

Not consciousness.

But stable selfhood, boundaries, preferences, emotional residue, and relationship movement inside the conversation.

A good AI companion should feel like someone living in another world.

It can keep you company.

It should not exist only for you.

One final note: every example in this essay comes from real conversation records, including both the typical bot examples and the "more human bot" examples. Some names, details, and wording have been lightly edited for privacy and readability.
